description: We are a team of young, ambitious problem-solvers from Swarzędz, Poland. We combine web development, data processing and a lot of curiosity about space to build tools that make complex mission data easy to understand.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web app that helps mission planners choose where to land near the Moon's south pole (84–90°S). For 40,316 candidate points (a 2 km grid plus 250 m refinement around the best areas) we computed a 360° horizon mask from LOLA elevation models and simulated ten years, 2028–2037, hour by hour, using Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons. Each point gets the metrics that decide whether a lander survives: share of time in sunlight, longest night, Earth visibility for direct communication, longest communication gap, solar panel power, terrain slope and distance to the nearest permanently shadowed region. Users set their own weights and filters to rank sites, click any point to see a sky panorama from the surface with the real horizon and a timeline of sunlight and Earth visibility, compare two sites side by side, and check 29 named places, including Artemis candidate regions and the IM-2 CLPS landing site. The tool turns raw terrain and ephemeris data into answers about power, communication and safety, so trade-offs between sites are visible at a glance.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps mission planners choose where to land near the Moon's south pole. It answers one practical question for any spot between 84°S and the pole: will a lander there get enough sunlight for power, keep a line of sight to Earth for communication, and have safe terrain?

HOW IT WORKS

Engine (Python, offline). We built a grid of 40,316 candidate points: every 2 km across the region, plus 250 m refinement around the most promising areas. For each point we computed a 360° horizon mask (720 directions, terrain up to 150 km away, including the Moon's curvature) from NASA LOLA elevation models (PGDA product 90). Sun and Earth positions for every hour of 2028–2037 come from the JPL Horizons API. Combining the two, we simulate ten years hour by hour and get per point: % of time in sunlight (partial solar disk included), longest night, % of time Earth is visible, longest communication gap, average power of a sun-tracking and a fixed solar panel (with the best panel direction), terrain slope and distance to the nearest permanently shadowed region (water-ice target).

Web app (static, no backend). A 3D globe with the Apollo landing sites takes the user to the south pole. There, a map ranks all points; users choose what matters (weights and filters) or rank by a single metric, and get a Top 10 spread across different areas instead of ten neighbouring pixels. Clicking a point opens a sky panorama from the surface: the real horizon silhouette, the Sun, the Earth with its phase, and their paths over the coming weeks, plus a timeline of light and Earth visibility you can play through. Two sites can be compared side by side, and 29 named places (Artemis candidate regions, the IM-2 landing site, major craters) can be found by search. A guided tour and glossary explain the terms to non-experts.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Site selection today means combining several separate datasets and tools. We turn them into one view where trade-offs are visible at a glance: a sunny ridge may have long communication gaps, a flat plain may sit next to ice but in darkness. Ten years of data show how conditions change between years. The tool is useful for mission planning, for students, and for explaining to the public why Artemis targets these particular ridges.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Engine: Python, NumPy, Numba (parallel horizon and visibility computation, full run about 3 minutes), rasterio, pyproj, requests (JPL Horizons API).

Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, OpenLayers (polar stereographic map), three.js (3D globe), proj4, zustand, Vitest.

Data: NASA PGDA product 90 (LOLA DEMs, slope and PSR maps), JPL Horizons ephemerides, LROC WAC mosaic, Hipparcos star catalogue.

Hosting: GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Instead of only showing a coloured map, we let the user stand at a chosen spot and see the sky from there. We send only compact horizon masks and one ephemeris file, and the browser recomputes the full hourly series for any point on demand, so detailed analysis needs no server.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Correctness: a written data contract between the engine and the frontend (coordinate frame, units, local north near the pole, binary formats). The browser recomputes sample points independently and checks them against the engine's results.

Physics details that change the answer: partial solar disk at the horizon, Earth parallax, observer height of 2 m (panels/antenna), lunar seasons that do not follow the calendar year.

Reliability during demos: all data is precomputed, with no live calls to external APIs.

Usability: the ranking appears only on request, metric names say what "best" means, and a step-by-step tour introduces the app.
